name: Battle of Issus

phases.title: The two armies draw up on either side of the river
phases.text: Alexander placed the Companions on his right and the Thessalian cavalry on the left of the phalanx under Parmenion. Darius set his heavy cavalry by the coast, the Greek mercenaries next, and the Cardaces along the river and into the foothills.

phases.title: The Persian cavalry charges across the river
phases.text: The Persian horse crossed the river and charged Parmenion and the allied cavalry. The Thessalian cavalry faced a larger mass of heavy horse and charged and fell back by turns to buy time.

phases.title: The Macedonian centre is thrown back
phases.text: The centre phalanx advanced across the river and up the fortified bank and suffered badly against the mercenaries. The Macedonians were forced to retreat across the river.

phases.title: The right wing breaks into the Persian line
phases.text: Alexander led the hypaspists on foot against the Cardaces and punched a hole through the Persian line. The Agrianians drove back the skirmishers on his far right, which secured the flank of the Companions.

phases.title: Alexander's cavalry attacks Darius, who flees
phases.text: Alexander mounted a horse at the head of the Companions and led a direct assault on Darius and his bodyguards. They fled from the battlefield.

phases.title: The Companions strike the mercenaries from behind
phases.text: Alexander saw his left flank and centre in trouble and let Darius go. He crashed into the rear of the Greek mercenaries, who broke up and began to retreat.

phases.title: The Persians abandon their positions
phases.text: The Persians saw that the Great King had gone and that the battle was being lost, and they fled in full rout. The Hellenic cavalry pursued them for as long as there was light.

note: The accounts do not say which way the Pinarus ran or where the camps stood, so the plan puts the sea at the top and the mountains at the foot, with the river between the armies. The Greek infantry and the hypaspists are placed between the cavalry wings as the course of the fighting implies; the accounts do not give their exact order of battle. The Persian line is drawn as a straight line; the accounts describe the Cardaces as wrapping across the river into the foothills.
